claims.text: A thin, conformal ALD-deposited alumina coating will significantly improve the corrosion resistance of stainless steel in extreme chloride-rich environments.
Conventional stainless steel has a native chromium-rich passive film.
Atomic Layer Deposition can be used to apply an alumina coating to stainless-steel surfaces.
Exposure to 3.5% NaCl solution at approximately 60°C represents an aggressive chloride-containing corrosion environment.
ALD will produce a uniform, defect-free, and tightly adherent alumina film on stainless steel.
The ALD-deposited alumina layer acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
The alumina layer limits chloride-ion penetration to the stainless-steel substrate.
The alumina layer limits oxygen penetration to the stainless-steel substrate.
Limiting chloride and oxygen penetration reduces localized breakdown of the underlying passive film.
Coated stainless steel will have a significantly lower corrosion current density than untreated stainless steel under identical conditions.
Coated stainless steel will exhibit increased electrochemical impedance relative to untreated stainless steel under identical conditions.
The corrosion-resistance benefit depends on the alumina coating remaining intact and adherent.
Severe mechanical wear or coating defects may diminish the corrosion-resistance benefit.
The long-term durability of the ALD coating under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses is not fully established.
The quantitative corrosion-resistance improvement may vary with coating parameters.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing untreated and ALD-alumina-coated stainless-steel samples after 100 hours in 3.5% NaCl at 60°C.
A corrosion-rate improvement of less than 30%, or premature loss of coating integrity, is designated as a falsifying result.
